newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bokassa death recalls bizarre Napoleonic crowning.
newsitem.headline: Bokassa death recalls bizarre Napoleonic crowning.

text.p: The African continent has known sorry scenes in the past but few as bizarre as the 1977 "Imperial" coronation of Emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa to the music of Mozart and jungle drums.

Modelling himself on the coronation garb of his hero Napoleon Bonaparte, Bokassa, who died on Sunday, wore a Roman emperor's toga when he was crowned emperor of the Central African Republic (renamed Empire).
Among a group of correspondents, I watched the ceremony in a suffocatingly hot indoor basketball stadium in his impoverished capital Bangui.
Bokassa arrived at the coronation in a lavish gilt carriage escorted by a troop of "Dragoons" on horseback, also in spectacular Napoleonic-era uniforms.
The horses danced nervously in the sweltering heat and several dragoons had trouble staying in the saddle and keeping their high "shako" hats from flying off into the bush.
Foreign envoys, sweating profusely in starched high white collars and black evening dress with tails, bowed and scraped as Bokassa entered accompanied by his dazzling young wife Catherine.

His bodyguards, fierce-looking soldiers who had recently "distinguished" themselves by cutting off the ears of prisoners in a public ceremony, levelled their sub-machine guns at the alarmed diplomats as they prowled the aisle.
The bodyguards were perhaps the only Central Africans invited to the coronation ceremony which cost a quarter of the the ex-Oubangui-Chari's foreign currency earnings of the year.

The local population, clad in rags and pressing forward out of curiosity in clouds of swirling red dust, was kept some 200 yards (metres) away by soldiers flailing at them with switches and heavily-studded belts.

Bangui had been turned inside out. Touring the city at dawn, reporters had come across yet another surreal scene: barefoot convicts wearing striped red-and-white jerseys and shorts struggling to unroll a giant red carpet on the main avenue.
Among the entertainers at the coronation was a troupe of Vietnamese dancers Bokassa had invited to recall his time as a sergeant in the French army during the first Indochina War of 1946-54.
"Dancers? Bullshit, they're hookers who got out of Saigon on time and now operate out of L.A. (Los Angeles)," an American bush pilot said in a bar after the coronation.
Two years later, Emperor Bokassa was overthrown, going off into exile in the Ivory Coast and later to France, before returning to face trial and prison.
One charge against him, never really substantiated, was that human meat was found in the coldroom of the palace kitchen when he was overthrown.

He still made news even out of power. Controversy over a present of diamonds he had made to president Valery Giscard d'Estaing was credited with being a reason why the French leader lost his bid for re-election in 1981.
On Bokassa's coronation day, I had stood at a window of the stadium, close to the carriage door when he emerged to enter.
He was about five metres away and stared unblinkingly ahead.
It's easy to say afterwards, but my initial thought was that his glazed look resembled that of a drug addict or a madman.
